USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 dinner with Xi to engage seriously on trade but without making new concessions. Hold the January 1 tariff increase as leverage. Signal willingness to delay the escalation if China offers substantive structural reforms on IP, tech transfer, and market access — but reject the 142-point list as insufficient. The US economy is strong enough to sustain current pressure; the goal now is to test whether China's deteriorating economy makes Xi willing to deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate and the balance of leverage favors Washington, warranting a negative threat score. The US economy is performing strongly — Q3 GDP at 3.5%, unemployment at a 50-year low of 3.7%, consumer confidence at 135.7 in November (Conference Board, Nov 27) — while China's economy is at its weakest since the 2009 financial crisis (Q3 GDP 6.5%, manufacturing PMI barely above contraction at 50.2 in October, new export orders contracting for five straight months, Shanghai Composite down ~25% YTD). The tariff asymmetry favors the US: China exports ~$506B to the US vs ~$130B US to China, limiting Beijing's ability to match duties dollar-for-dollar (Business Insider, Nov 9). Three rounds of US tariffs ($250B at 10%) are already in effect with matching Chinese retaliation, but the real bite comes January 1 when List 3 rises to 25% — and Chinese exporters are front-loading shipments now, meaning a sharper cliff awaits in Q1 2019 (Politico, Oct 31; Moody's estimate of 1.2pp GDP hit if 25% tariffs go to full coverage).

However, the US faces real domestic costs that counsel against unchecked escalation. The stock market has erased all 2018 gains — S&P 500 fell 1.8% on Nov 20 alone, Dow down 552 points, FAANG stocks in bear market territory (CNBC, Nov 20; NYT, Nov 20). GM announced significant layoffs this week. Trade dragged on Q3 GDP by the most in 33 years (Business Insider). The IMF downgraded global growth forecasts, explicitly citing US trade wars (The Hill, Oct 9). Farm-belt states face Chinese retaliation on soybeans and agriculture. Tariffs are raising costs for American importers and small businesses ahead of the holiday season (CNN, Nov 19).

The G20 meeting in Buenos Aires (Nov 30-Dec 1) is the only scheduled Trump-Xi encounter before the January 1 deadline. Pre-meeting signals are mixed: Chinese negotiators canceled Washington visits after a war of words at APEC, where Pence warned the US would 'more than double' tariffs and the summit failed to produce a joint communique for the first time in 25 years (CNBC, Nov 19; Guardian, Nov 25). Yet Trump has signaled a new willingness to deal, and Kudlow says 'there's a good possibility we can make a deal' (NYT, Nov 27). The internal White House divide between hardliners (Navarro, Lighthizer) and moderates (Mnuchin, Kudlow) will shape the outcome. The US should negotiate from its current position of strength — strong economy, Chinese weakness, January deadline as leverage — rather than escalate further into a situation where domestic market damage erodes the political foundation for the trade policy.

China economy weakening: slowest GDP since 2009 (6.5%), manufacturing PMI barely above contraction (50.2), export orders contracting 5 months
US stock market erased 2018 gains; S&P 500 in correction territory, FAANG in bear market
Jan 1 deadline: List 3 tariffs rise from 10% to 25% on $200B of Chinese goods
APEC summit failed to produce joint communique for first time in 25 years
Chinese trade delegation canceled Washington visits ahead of G20
Internal WH divisions: hardliners (Navarro/Lighthizer) vs moderates (Mnuchin/Kudlow)
China's 142-point concession list rejected by Trump as 'not acceptable'
Tariff asymmetry limits China's retaliation capacity ($506B exports vs $130B imports)
IMF downgraded global growth, explicitly citing US trade wars

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports
Trump could seek a China trade truce at G-20 despite tough talk. Behind his tough talk is a creeping anxiety about the costs of a prolonged trade war on the financial markets and the broader economy
APEC summit ended without agreement on a joint communique, breaking a 25-year tradition. Pence warned Beijing that Trump wasn't in a rush to end the trade war
Chinese delegation cancelled plans to visit Washington. Trump described China's 142 concessions as 'not acceptable'
